Project Overview

Lightweight VPN

Bring WireGuard to NuttX-based microcontrollers.

Virtual interface

Secure communication

Takeaway

PART 1 · 1/55 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Here is the whole project in one picture.

I brought WireGuard, a lightweight VPN, to Apache NuttX. It appears as a virtual network interface called wg0, next to the normal network interface. Packets sent to wg0 are encrypted and travel over a UDP socket, and the other side can be any normal WireGuard peer. So a NuttX microcontroller can exchange IP packets securely.

PART 1 · 3/57 / 35

Now, what is Apache NuttX?

NuttX is a POSIX-like real-time operating system for small devices. It has a small footprint, and it supports a very wide range of hardware: more than fifteen CPU architectures and more than three hundred boards. It is also an Apache top-level project, developed in the open.

FreeRTOS and Zephyr are good RTOSes too. The difference I care about is the API. NuttX is POSIX-like by design, with pthreads, sockets, files and a shell. That is why a VPN can become a normal network device here.

And it is not a toy. Sony uses it in audio products and SPRESENSE. Fitbit used it in fitness trackers, such as the Charge 3 and Charge 4. PX4 drone flight controllers run on it. Xiaomi's OpenVela is reported to run on more than a thousand products. And a small lunar robot, SORA-Q, used it on Japan's 2024 Moon mission. Next, Sony's own history with NuttX.

This is Sony's history with NuttX. It is not my story yet, and it is older than edge AI.

The public record starts in 2013, when Sony engineers began porting NuttX to the LC823425 audio processor. Bluetooth and LC823450 followed in 2014, and the first commercial audio products shipped in 2015. Public examples include the Walkman NW-WS620, the SMR-10 personal sound amplifier, and the ICD-TX800 and ICD-PX470 voice recorders.

In 2018, Xperia Ear Duo shipped with Sony's CXD5602 and NuttX, while SPRESENSE made the same multicore platform available as a development board with GNSS, audio and camera support. In 2019 and 2020, Sony engineers documented the work and moved substantial CXD56xx platform and driver support upstream. In the 2020s, the platform's capabilities continued to expand across camera, GNSS, connectivity and edge sensing. That last point is about technical capability, not a claim that every feature shipped in a named product.

That is the background. Part two: the problem, and the solution I chose.

Problem: How Can We Securely Access Remote Devices?

Devices are far away

Embedded devices sit at remote sites and on other networks.

Remote diagnosis

Engineers need to check and fix them when something goes wrong.

A secure path

Wi-Fi security protects the radio link. Remote access needs its own secure path.

Takeaway

We needed a secure way to access and troubleshoot remote NuttX devices.

PART 2 · 1/411 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Now, the problem I wanted to solve.

Embedded devices are often installed far away: at a customer's site, in a factory, or on another network. When something goes wrong, an engineer wants to log in, check the device, and fix it, without traveling there.

Wi-Fi security, WPA2 or WPA3, protects the radio link between the device and the access point. That is important, but it is only one hop. It does not give an engineer a way to reach the device across the Internet. For that, we need a secure path of its own, all the way from the engineer to the device. The same need appears in edge AI, industrial IoT, and many other remote systems.

So the question is: how can we securely access remote devices? Let's look at the options.

Options: Ways to Reach a Remote Device

WayAny IP service (telnet, web…)?No server in the middle?Protected up to
Open a port to the Internetyesyesthe application itself
HTTPS / MQTT via a cloudno, only your API or messagesno, a server or brokerthe server or broker
Reverse tunnel / relay (SSH, WebSocket)one port per tunnelno, a relay hostthe relay host
VPN on the routeryes, the whole LANyesthe router, not the LAN behind it
Carrier closed networkyesno, the carrierthe carrier gateway
VPN on the device (this talk)yes, any IP serviceyes, any WireGuard peerthe device itself
Takeaway

Every option has trade-offs. I chose a VPN on the device, so the device itself is the end of the tunnel.

Each option can be made secure. The last column shows where its protection ends. Mesh VPN agents (Tailscale, ZeroTier) are another “VPN on the device” option, but they usually need a bigger OS.
PART 2 · 2/412 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

There are several ways to access a remote device: open a port, use a cloud API or an MQTT broker, set up a reverse tunnel, or use a VPN on the router.

Each approach has its own trade-offs. HTTPS and MQTT are great for sending data, but they do not give you a shell or a web page on the device. A router VPN works well when the router is yours, but the protection ends at the router. None of them is bad, and all of them can be made secure. They just protect different parts of the path.

For this project, I wanted something different: a standard VPN that runs directly on the NuttX device, so the device itself is the end of the tunnel. That is the solution.

Solution: A VPN on the Device

Why WireGuard?

Small & simple

Far less code than IPsec or OpenVPN, so it is easier to review and to port.

Lines of code, 2018 — not today's counts
Modern cryptography

ChaCha20-Poly1305 and Curve25519, in one fixed, well-defined suite.

UDP-based tunnel

Encrypted IP packets over UDP. It works with existing WireGuard peers such as Linux, and the microcontroller itself is the VPN endpoint.

Takeaway

Run a lightweight, standard VPN directly on the NuttX device.

Lines of code (rounded): J. Donenfeld, “WireGuard”, Linux Plumbers Conference 2018, wireguard.com/talks/lpc2018-wireguard-slides.pdf. Specific implementations, counted in 2018; the talk's own slides differ slightly for OpenVPN.
PART 2 · 3/413 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

So, my solution: put a VPN on the device itself.

Why WireGuard? First, it is small and simple. In a talk in 2018, its author compared lines of code: about four thousand for WireGuard, about a hundred and twenty thousand for OpenVPN, and over four hundred thousand for IPsec with strongSwan. These are old numbers for specific implementations, but the gap is large, and it matters on a microcontroller.

Second, modern cryptography: ChaCha20-Poly1305 and Curve25519. I will not go into the details here. Third, it is a tunnel over plain UDP. Each peer is known by its public key, and the packets are normal UDP, so the device can talk to existing WireGuard peers, such as Linux or Windows. The microcontroller itself becomes the end of the tunnel.

So the idea is simple: run a lightweight, standard VPN directly on the NuttX device. Next, where wg0 sits inside NuttX.

Architecture: where wg0 sits

Takeaway

To NuttX, wg0 is a normal network device. Under it, WireGuard turns its packets into encrypted UDP.

PART 2 · 4/414 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

This is one step more technical than the overview. This is where the implementation starts.

Going out, a packet comes down from the application through TCP or UDP and IP, and reaches wg0 like any other network device. WireGuard encrypts it, and it leaves as a UDP packet — through wlan0 on a board, or through usrsock when the Wi-Fi chip itself works through sockets. Coming in is the same path the other way: a UDP packet arrives, WireGuard decrypts it, and it is passed up to wg0 as if it came in on a normal interface.

From here on, the work is building this middle part — wg0 and the encryption — without changing the layers above or below it.

Part three: the development plan. How do we start from an existing WireGuard?

Porting Strategy: Start from wireguard-lwip

STARTING POINTgithub.com/smartalock/wireguard-lwipAn existing open-source WireGuard for lwIP
KEEP

Protocol & crypto

Reuse the WireGuard protocol and cryptography, with two small fixes.

ADAPT

Platform hooks

Implement NuttX-specific system functions.

REPLACE

lwIP network glue

Use NuttX networking APIs instead of lwIP.

Takeaway

We ported wireguard-lwip to NuttX by reusing the core, adapting platform hooks, and replacing the lwIP integration.

PART 3 · 1/216 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Now the plan. I did not write WireGuard from scratch.

I started from wireguard-lwip, an open-source WireGuard implementation for the lwIP network stack. The link is on the slide. It already has the protocol and the cryptography, so I could focus on the porting work.

I sorted the code into three parts. First, the protocol and crypto: the handshake, the data transport, and the crypto primitives. I kept them. The crypto is used as it is, and the protocol core needed two small fixes, which I found later in a review. Second, the platform hooks. Everything that depends on the OS sits behind one small header, as four functions: a monotonic clock, random bytes, the current time in TAI64N format, and a check for whether the system is under load. I adapted these to NuttX. Third, the lwIP glue. NuttX does not have lwIP, so I replaced this layer. That is the real porting work.

Next: how the lwIP ideas map to NuttX.

Mapping lwIP Networking to NuttX

ConceptlwIPNuttX
Network devicestruct netifstruct net_driver_s
Packet bufferspbufiob (d_iob)
Registrationnetif_add()netdev_register()
Sendingoutput callbackd_txavail → devif_poll()
UDP “wire”udp_pcb, udp_sendto()UDP socket, psock_sendto()

These are matches of ideas, not a one-to-one swap of APIs.

Takeaway

Porting meant using NuttX's own building blocks, not bringing lwIP into NuttX.

PART 3 · 2/217 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

This was the most important porting decision.

Instead of bringing lwIP into NuttX, I matched each lwIP idea to a NuttX building block. lwIP's network interface becomes a NuttX net_driver_s. lwIP's packet buffer, pbuf, corresponds to NuttX's I/O buffer, iob. Adding an interface becomes registering a device, and I register wg0 as a tunnel-type device. Where lwIP calls an output callback to send a packet, NuttX calls the driver's txavail function, and the driver polls the stack with devif_poll. The wire under wg0 is a plain UDP socket.

These are matches of ideas, not a one-to-one swap of APIs. The point is simple: use NuttX's own parts. Next, Version 1, the first working tunnel.

PART 4 · 1/519 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Version 1 put WireGuard into NuttX as an application, in a FLAT build. The goal was a standard tunnel that could be configured at run time, without rebuilding the firmware.

This table shows how much work each layer needed. About three thousand lines of protocol and crypto came over from wireguard-lwip. The crypto came over exactly as it was. The protocol core needed two small fixes after a review, and one of them was a bug in wireguard-lwip itself: its rate limit never worked. The four OS functions are small, about a hundred and twenty lines. The real work was the network glue: the netdev, the UDP socket, and the receive task. In the first working tunnel, that was about twelve hundred new lines.

The result was a working tunnel. That proved the approach, but it also exposed OS and networking problems that a first successful ping could not show. Let me show you where it was hard.

Where it was hard: six bugs

#BugShowed up inLesson
1The receive thread stopped when the wg command exitedapps versionpthread_detach() frees memory later. It does not keep a thread alive.
2ping works, TCP dies in detailapps versionA file descriptor belongs to one task group.
3“No real impact” was 10× in detailapps versionMeasure a quick fix before you call it free.
4Stack 94% full; saving the config froze the boardreal boards only, never simMeasure on real hardware. Sim's big stacks hide it.
5Handshake OK, data fails: NuttX's own ChaCha20‑Poly1305 part 5kernel driverA passing handshake does not prove the data path.
6A 6 KB array on a 3 KB kernel stack part 5BUILD_KERNEL (QEMU)The same stack lesson, one level deeper.
Takeaway

Most of them hid behind a test that passed, so I first looked in the wrong place.

PART 4 · 2/520 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Now, where it was hard.

The first tunnel worked quickly. Most of my time went into six bugs: four in the apps version, and two more after I moved it into the kernel. Most of them hid behind a test that passed, like a handshake or a ping, so I first looked in the wrong place.

Bug one: the receive thread was created as detached, and it stopped when the wg command that started it exited. Detach only decides when the memory is freed, not how long the thread lives. That is why, in the kernel version, the driver owns its thread. Bug four: only real hardware showed it. On the board, the receive task's stack was ninety-four percent full, with only 176 bytes left. Sim has big stacks, so it never saw it. Please remember this one.

I will tell two of them in detail, because their lessons are useful for anyone. Bugs five and six come in part five. The logs and fixes for all six are in the GitHub repository.

Bug ②: Ping Works. TCP Dies.

SYMPTOM

ping works: 0% loss.

A TCP handshake even completes, then the connection dies.

psock_sendto: ret=-1 errno=9
EBADF — “Bad file descriptor”

ROOT CAUSE & FIX

Sends from the wg_rx task worked. Sends from the system work queue, which flushes TCP data, failed.

Cause: a file descriptor belongs to one task group. It is not valid in another one.

Fix: use psock_*() on a struct socket. No fd, so any task can use it.

Takeaway

If only some tasks fail, look at what each task owns. Here, it was the file descriptor.

PART 4 · 3/521 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

This is my favorite bug in the project.

On the same tunnel, ping was perfect, and even a TCP handshake finished, and then the connection died. When I added logging to the send path, it showed EBADF: bad file descriptor. All the sends that worked happened inside the receive task itself: handshake replies, keepalives, ping replies, the SYN-ACK, which is the second step of a TCP connection. The sends that failed came from the system work queue, which sends the TCP application data later.

The reason: in NuttX, a file descriptor belongs to the task group that opened it. The file descriptor was not broken. It was just not visible from another task group. The fix was to stop using file descriptors and use NuttX's internal socket API. It works on a struct socket, which is just memory, so any task can use it. That is exactly why the kernel version keeps the socket as a struct socket.

Bug ③: “No Real Impact” Was 10× Slower

QUICK FIX

Check every 50 ms

Dropping fds also broke poll(), so I polled the socket. I thought the only cost was waking an idle CPU.

Measured: about 10× slower.

REAL FIX

Event-driven wake-up

A callback on psock_poll() and a semaphore: a real blocking wait. Each packet wakes the thread when it arrives.

Takeaway

A quick fix you never measure can look free. Measure it.

PART 4 · 4/522 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

The third: something I never measured.

The fix without file descriptors also broke poll, because poll works with file descriptors. So, as a quick fix, I checked the socket every fifty milliseconds. I thought the only cost was waking up the CPU when it was idle. I was wrong. Every packet that arrived waited up to fifty milliseconds, and that alone limited the speed: about ten times slower than it should have been. I thought it had no real cost, and it cost ten times.

The real fix was a proper wait. The socket calls back and a semaphore wakes the thread up when data arrives.

PART 4 · 5/523 / 35

That was Version 1. Part five, the harder half: a real kernel driver, and how I checked it.

Version 2: WireGuard as a NuttX kernel driver

BEFORE — VERSION 1

An application

Lives in apps/ and reaches into kernel internals (psock_*).

Works only in a FLAT build, and does not fit as an in-tree driver.

AFTER — VERSION 2

A kernel driver

wg0 lives in drivers/net/wireguard/. A small wg command sets it up through ioctl.

Made for FLAT, PROTECTED and KERNEL builds.

BUILD MODES

FLATApplications and kernel share one address space.
PROTECTEDMPU separates application and kernel memory.
KERNELMMU provides separate address spaces.
Takeaway

The goal: a proper kernel driver for every NuttX build mode, in a form that is easier to review upstream.

PART 5 · 1/425 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Why did I move it into the kernel?

Version 1 is an application. It lives in apps and reaches into socket internals of the kernel. That works in a FLAT build, where applications and the kernel share one address space. But it does not fit as an in-tree driver, and it cannot work in PROTECTED or KERNEL builds, where applications and the kernel are kept apart. In PROTECTED builds, the MPU separates their memory. In KERNEL builds, the MMU gives each side its own address space.

So I moved the device into the kernel, next to the other network drivers, and a small wg command sets it up through ioctl, which stands for input/output control. Version 1 showed that the protocol works on NuttX. Version 2 is about fitting NuttX itself: a normal driver for every build mode, in a form that is easier for the community to review. That does not mean it will be accepted. It means it follows how NuttX is built.

The Kernel Design: The Big Picture

Takeaway

The driver owns everything that must keep running. The command only sends settings, and then it can exit.

PART 5 · 2/426 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

This is the shape of the real driver. The top is user space, the bottom is the NuttX kernel.

In user space, there is only a small wg command. It sends settings to the kernel through ioctl. Each ioctl carries one flat struct with no pointers inside, so in PROTECTED and KERNEL builds the kernel never has to follow a pointer into user memory. The private key is write-only: no ioctl ever gives it back.

In the kernel, wg0 is a normal network device. It owns its UDP socket and its receive thread, so the thread and socket bugs from Version 1 cannot happen, by design. The crypto is NuttX's own. The protocol core is still derived from wireguard-lwip under BSD-3-Clause, and the LICENSE file says so.

Two Issues Found During Kernel Integration

CRYPTOGRAPHY — ChaCha20-Poly1305

NuttX crypto/chachapoly.c

  • The nonce counter sits in different bytes from the RFC 8439 / WireGuard layout.
  • Counter 0 still matches: the handshake works, but data packets after the first fail.
  • A two-line fix with test vectors, kept as its own change.
KERNEL STACK — Stack Overflow

This driver, KERNEL build only

  • Setting the peers put a 6 KB array on a 3 KB kernel stack: overflow, then panic.
  • The sim (FLAT, big stacks) never showed it.
  • A bug in the driver itself. The array now lives on the heap.
Takeaway

Porting WireGuard also surfaced findings worth sharing with the NuttX community.

PART 5 · 3/427 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

On the way into the kernel, I found two separate problems.

The first is in NuttX's ChaCha20-Poly1305 code. The 64-bit counter goes into different bytes of the nonce from the layout in RFC 8439, which WireGuard uses. When the counter is zero, both layouts give the same bytes. So the handshake works, and then the data packets after the first one fail to decrypt. The fix is two lines. I prepared it as a separate crypto change with test vectors, and as far as I can see, current master still has the same layout.

The second is a bug in my own driver, not in NuttX. Setting the peers put a six-kilobyte array on a three-kilobyte kernel stack, and that caused a panic, only in a KERNEL build. The simulator has big stacks, so it never showed. I moved the array to the heap. It is the same stack lesson as Bug 4, one level deeper.

One more finding from the board side, which I left off the slide: on NuttX 13.0.1 and master, SPRESENSE did not boot with the high-resolution RTC option, CONFIG_RTC_HIRES. I found the cause and fixed it locally. The report is drafted, but not filed yet.

I prepared these as small, separate pieces, so they are easy for the community to review. Nothing is submitted yet.

Takeaway

Verified on real boards in FLAT builds and on QEMU in KERNEL / PROTECTED builds.Real-hardware testing for those modes remains open.

PART 5 · 4/428 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Let me be exact about which build mode ran where. There are three, and I keep them apart.

FLAT, on real boards. On October 12, I ran the exact series I prepared for upstream on the ESP32-S3 inside the StackChan: a handshake with Linux WireGuard, and ping both ways, up to the full packet size. An earlier build of the driver ran on both boards over real Wi-Fi with the Windows client. On SPRESENSE I measured memory: after forty down-and-up cycles, it was exactly the same. The receive thread used 1,472 bytes of a six-kilobyte default. That default used to be a guess. Now it is a measurement.

KERNEL, in QEMU. The wg command is a separate program that reaches the driver through system calls, and the tunnel reaches Linux. With four CPUs, I flooded it while changing the settings. No fault, but that is one scripted run, not a full search for race conditions.

PROTECTED, also in QEMU. The tunnel works, and every ioctl crosses the memory boundary. Repeated runs sometimes faulted. The cause was a stack overflow in the wg command, because in this mode a system call runs on the caller's own stack. A bigger default fixed it: twenty out of twenty.

What I have not shown is KERNEL or PROTECTED on real hardware. I tried PROTECTED on the CoreS3, but that board does not boot any bootloader-based image, and that is not a WireGuard problem. So the check marks mean: it passed in these conditions. They are not a promise for every board. The records are on GitHub.

PART 6 · 1/130 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

This is the live demo. I keep this slide on the screen, and the terminal is next to it.

First the setup. My laptop and the Stack-chan are both on my smartphone's Wi-Fi hotspot. The phone only provides the local network. Between the laptop and the Stack-chan there is one WireGuard tunnel: the laptop is 10.10.0.1, and the Stack-chan, running Apache NuttX, is 10.10.0.2. The phone is not a WireGuard peer. It only carries encrypted UDP.

Step 1, the VPN connection. On the laptop I run wg show. You should see the peer, a latest handshake, an endpoint on the phone's network, and the transfer counters.

Step 2, remote login. I run telnet to 10.10.0.2, the address inside the tunnel. You should see the NuttX shell prompt.

Step 3, the network interface. I run ifconfig. You should see wlan0 on the phone's network, and wg0 with 10.10.0.2. So I am really logged in through the tunnel.

Step 4, control. I run stackchan face happy, and the face changes. The other expressions are neutral, sad, angry, sleepy and surprised. Then I run stackchan say with the address of a voice clip on the laptop, http://10.10.0.1:8000/hello.wav. The clip comes through the same tunnel, and the Stack-chan speaks and moves its mouth. I made the clips on the laptop in advance, so there is no cloud API.

If there is time, the packets. In another terminal, the packet capture on the phone's network shows only encrypted UDP on port 51820. The capture inside the tunnel shows the telnet text in plain text. Then wg show again: the byte counts went up.

This robot runs the application build in a FLAT build. The kernel driver ran on the same ESP32-S3 in the testing part, but this robot demo is built on the application. What I want you to take away: a NuttX device, controlled remotely through WireGuard. Now, the summary.

PART 7 · 1/432 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

To sum up. We brought WireGuard to Apache NuttX. A NuttX device can now talk to standard WireGuard peers over an encrypted IP tunnel.

We developed it from an application into a kernel network driver. We tested it on real boards, and on QEMU in the kernel build modes.

Next, I am preparing the driver and the related fixes for review by the NuttX community. They are small, separate pieces, and nothing is submitted yet. That is the technical story. Now, a few things I learned.

What I learned

Lesson 1

From application user to OS contributor

For years I used NuttX from the application side.

This time I worked inside the OS: drivers and the kernel.

Lesson 2

AI helped me code, but understanding was my job

I used Claude a lot. Research and code went much faster.

OS internals were new to me. I did not take AI code as it was. I asked, read, and tested until I could explain it myself.

That was the hard part.

Lesson 3

A welcoming open-source community

Good docs and contributing guides. Active discussion and review.

Open to AI-assisted development, with people staying responsible.

CI, hackathons and events help new people join.

Hope

I hope to keep contributing to Apache NuttX and the open-source community, and I look forward to seeing NuttX continue to grow.

PART 7 · 2/433 / 35
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

That was the technical part. Now, three things I learned.

First, I came to NuttX as an application developer. This time I worked inside the OS: drivers and the kernel.

Second, and I want to say this one clearly. I used AI, Claude, a lot in this project. It made research and writing code much faster. But embedded OS internals were new to me, and really understanding the design and the behavior was hard. I could not just take the code the AI wrote. I had to ask questions, read the NuttX source, test the behavior, and keep going until I could explain it myself. AI helped me code, but understanding was my job.

Third, the community. NuttX has good documentation and contributing guides, and active technical discussion and review. It is open to AI-assisted development, but people stay responsible: a commit says Assisted-by, and AI never adds a Signed-off-by. And CI and hackathons help new people join. Open source is not only code that is public. It grows when new people can join, learn, and contribute.

I hope to keep contributing to Apache NuttX and the open-source community, and I look forward to seeing NuttX continue to grow.

Testing: What Ping Misses

Same key on every boot?

SPRESENSE 3 resets, 3 different keys.

A quick check, not a proof of good randomness.

Keys left in memory after down?

sim session keys all zero after down.

The static key stays, on purpose, so up works again.

A leak that shows after hours?

sim 151 rekeys, 100 down/up: nothing lost.

Memory back to the start-up count. Not a week-long run.

Takeaway

Each risk needs its own test. A passing tunnel is not one of them.

APPENDIXA1 / A2
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Appendix, for questions. This slide is about what a working tunnel cannot tell you: three problems that ping would never notice.

First, keys. NuttX can seed its random device from build-time settings. Then a board makes the same private key every time it starts, and everything still works. So I reset a SPRESENSE three times and got three different keys. That is a quick check, not a proof of good randomness.

Second, I read the device's memory in the simulator. After down, the session keys were all zero. The static key stays on purpose, so that up works again.

Third, a long test, also in the simulator: a hundred and fifty-one forced rekeys and a hundred down-and-up cycles. No buffer was lost, and memory went back to exactly the start-up number. I am not saying it ran for a week, or that the simulator acts like the board.

Design Choice: Trust the Clock?

Each handshake needs a newer timestamp than the peer has seen, even after a reboot.

Chosen

Real-time clock + the highest value used this boot. Same rule as Linux and wireguard-go, plus a warning when the clock was never set.

Not chosen

Save every timestamp: wears out flash.
Reserve a range in flash: needs a write guarantee I could not verify.
Wait: as long as it last ran.

Same board, nothing sent to it: clock unset → no handshake in 75 s. Clock set → 4.1 s.

Takeaway

Without a clock, a device may not reconnect by itself, and a ping test will not show it.

APPENDIXA2 / A2
October 11–14, 2026Glasgow, Scotland

Appendix, for questions. This is the one place where I had to decide, not test. And then I measured my decision.

WireGuard's replay protection has a rule: every handshake needs a newer timestamp than the peer has seen, even after a reboot. The device is usually the side that starts the handshake, and it is also the side least likely to have a clock with a battery.

Saving every timestamp wears out the flash. Reserving a range in flash is the right long-term answer, but it needs a write guarantee I could not verify on these file systems. And just waiting means a device that ran for a month cannot reconnect for a month. Here, the easy choice and the right choice were not the same.

So I chose the real-time clock plus the highest value used in this boot, exactly what Linux and wireguard-go do. And the driver warns once if the clock was never set.

Then I measured it on the board. I sent the board nothing at all, because a ping from the peer would start the handshake for it. With the clock as it boots: no handshake in a seventy-five-second watch. With the clock set: four point one seconds. That is why the driver prints a warning.
